content: 1. The challenges and future directions in managing infectious diseases, including HIV, were discussed in a 2017 study published in Epidemiology and Infection. This study emphasized the importance of addressing gaps in surveillance and program evaluation to improve outcomes. 2. A 2020 study by Etoori et al., published in Frontiers in Public Health, highlighted the issue of misreporting patient outcomes in South Africa's National HIV Treatment Database. The study underscored the consequences of such inaccuracies for program planning, monitoring, and evaluation. 3. Bogoch et al. (2018) explored the use of verbal autopsy to identify gaps in the HIV care continuum. Their findings, published in The Lancet HIV, demonstrated the potential of this method to improve care delivery and outcomes. 4. Pantazis et al. (2021) investigated the distinction between pre-migration and post-migration HIV acquisition using surveillance data. Their research, published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, provided insights into migration-related HIV risks. 5. A 2019 evidence synthesis by Presanis et al. examined trends in undiagnosed HIV infections in England and their implications for achieving HIV elimination by 2030. This study emphasized the need for targeted interventions to address these trends. 6. The Pan American Health Organization (2019) developed a framework for monitoring HIV and STI services for key populations in Latin America and the Caribbean. This framework aims to enhance service delivery and data quality. 7. A data quality assessment tool for national and partner HIV treatment and patient monitoring systems was introduced by the World Health Organization (WHO). This tool supports the implementation of robust data systems to improve program performance. 8. The WHO's 2020 report, Prevailing Against Pandemics by Putting People at the Centre, emphasized the importance of person-centered approaches in combating pandemics, including HIV. 9. Rice et al. (2012) proposed a novel method to assign the country of HIV infection among heterosexual individuals born abroad. This method, published in AIDS, aimed to improve the accuracy of epidemiological data. 10. Holmes et al. (2019) evaluated the benefits of routine opt-out HIV testing and linkage-to-care programs in publicly funded emergency departments in Houston, Texas. Their findings highlighted the effectiveness of such programs in improving care for previously diagnosed patients. 11. De Schacht et al. (2014) reported high rates of HIV seroconversion among pregnant women and low levels of HIV testing among male partners in southern Mozambique. Their mixed-methods study, published in PLOS One, called for enhanced testing strategies. 12. Rosinska et al. (2018) proposed a methodology to adjust for missing data and reporting delays in the European Union's HIV Surveillance System. This approach aimed to improve the accuracy of HIV incidence estimates. 13. Cori et al. (2015) examined CD4+ cell dynamics in untreated HIV-1 infection, considering factors such as age, viral load, sex, and calendar time. Their study, published in AIDS, provided valuable insights into disease progression. 14. Johnson et al. (2015) analyzed HIV testing and diagnosis rates in South Africa, identifying successes and challenges in the country's response to the epidemic. 15. Presanis et al. (2021) synthesized evidence on undiagnosed HIV prevalence trends in England, emphasizing the need for targeted strategies to eliminate HIV transmission by 2030. 16. Szwarcwald et al. (2015) estimated HIV incidence and the number of people living with HIV/AIDS in Brazil. Their findings highlighted the importance of ageand sex-specific data for effective epidemic management. 17. 18. Flash et al. (2015) demonstrated the benefits of routine opt-out HIV testing programs in emergency departments, emphasizing their role in improving linkage to care. 19. The WHO's 2022 consolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis, and STI prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations provided comprehensive recommendations for public health approaches. 20. Harichund et al. (2019) investigated repeat HIV testing practices in the era of self-testing among adults in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Their study, published in PLOS One, highlighted the importance of repeat testing for early detection. 21. Regan et al. (2013) identified factors associated with self-reported repeat HIV testing after a negative result in Durban, South Africa. Their findings emphasized the need for targeted interventions to encourage retesting. 22. Jacob et al. (2020) explored the utility of digitizing point-of-care HIV test results to improve performance toward UNAIDS 90-90-90 targets. Their study, published in PLOS One, demonstrated the potential of digital tools in enhancing data accuracy. 23. Jones et al. (2020) analyzed trends in HIV testing and seroconversion among female sex workers in Zimbabwe's national Sisters program. Their findings highlighted the importance of targeted interventions for this population. 24. Brizzi et al. (2021) used modeling to track the elimination of HIV transmission among men who have sex with men in England. Their study, published in The Lancet HIV, provided valuable insights into progress toward this goal. 25. Nwokolo et al. (2017) reported a rapid decline in HIV infections among men who have sex with men in central London. Their findings underscored the effectiveness of targeted prevention strategies. 26. Ehrenkranz et al. (2021) proposed revising the HIV service delivery cascade to achieve UNAIDS 95-95-95 goals. Their study, published in PLOS Medicine, emphasized the need for innovative approaches to care. 27. Paschen-Wolff et al. (2019) conducted a systematic review of interventions promoting frequent HIV testing. Their findings, published in AIDS Behavior, highlighted effective strategies to increase testing rates. 28. Rice et al. (2018) emphasized the importance of strengthening routine data systems to track the HIV epidemic and guide responses in sub-Saharan Africa. Their study, published in JMIR Public Health Surveillance, called for improved data quality and use. 29. Rentsch et al. (2017) introduced a software tool for linking demographic surveillance and health facility data. This tool, known as Point-of-Contact Interactive Record Linkage (PIRL), aimed to enhance data integration and analysis. 30. Ayoub et al. (2018) demonstrated the use of routine HIV testing data for early detection of emerging epidemics in high-risk populations. Their concept study highlighted the potential of such data for targeted interventions. 31. Sheng et al. (2017) developed statistical models to incorporate routine HIV testing data from antenatal clinics into epidemic estimates. Their study, published in AIDS, provided a framework for improving HIV surveillance. 32. Hargreaves et al. (2016) analyzed program data to estimate HIV incidence and service uptake among female sex workers in Zimbabwe. Their findings emphasized the importance of targeted interventions for this population. 33. Grabbe et al. (2015) examined retesting and seroconversion rates among HIV testing clients in Lesotho. Their study highlighted the need for repeat testing to improve early detection. 34. Osmond et al. (1994) investigated HIV infection rates among young homosexual and bisexual men in San Francisco. Their findings provided valuable insights into the epidemic's dynamics in this population. 35. Van Griensven et al. (2018) validated a behavioral imputation algorithm for estimating recent HIV incidence among young men who have sex with men. Their study emphasized the importance of accurate surveillance methods. 36. The WHO's 2022 update on recency assays for HIV surveillance provided guidance on their use for estimating population-level HIV incidence. 37. Galiwango et al. (2021) validated the Asante HIV-1 rapid recency assay for detecting recent infections in Uganda. Their findings supported the assay's use in surveillance programs. 38. Grebe et al. (2019) developed an international external quality assurance program for HIV-1 incidence using the Limiting Antigen Avidity assay. Their study emphasized the importance of quality assurance in surveillance. 39. Abdool Karim et al. (2020) discussed the ethical considerations of disclosing HIV recency testing results to individuals. 40. TRACE, a program for tracking HIV epidemics using recency assays, provided valuable insights into epidemic control strategies. 42.
